message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Business Case: Self-Checkout Expansion
Northfield Grocers, prepared for the Executive Committee, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper asks the Executive Committee to approve capital of £1.34 million to install self-checkout lanes in the 14 Northfield stores that do not yet have them, bringing all 18 stores onto the same front-end format by the end of Q3 2026. The recommendation rests on a ten-month pilot in four stores, which began in May 2025.

2. Background
Front-end labour is our second-largest controllable cost after stock. Staffed checkout hours have risen 9% over two years while transaction counts have been flat, largely because of minimum-wage increases and the difficulty of rostering part-time staff for evening peaks. Queue length is also the most frequent complaint in our customer feedback system, cited in 31% of negative comments in 2025.

The four pilot stores (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley) were chosen because they had been fully refurbished in early 2025 and had the floor space to accommodate a six-kiosk bank without removing shelving. Each received six kiosks and retained two staffed lanes.

3. Pilot results
Across the three pilot stores, the key results after ten months were:

Metric | Pilot stores | Other stores
Staffed checkout hours per week (change) | -95 hours per store | +3 hours per store
Average queue time at peak | 2.1 min (from 4.6) | 4.4 min (from 4.5)
Shrink as % of sales | 1.2% (from 1.2%) | 1.3% (from 1.3%)
Average basket value (change) | +6% | +2%
Customer satisfaction, front end (index) | 78 (from 71) | 72 (from 72)

The reduction in staffed hours was achieved without redundancies, through natural turnover and redeployment of colleagues into online order picking. Shrink did not move, which addresses the main concern raised when the pilot was approved. Front-end satisfaction rose seven points in the pilot stores and was flat elsewhere.

The rise in average basket value is the most encouraging result. Basket value grew three times as fast in the pilot stores as in the rest of the estate, which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit. We have not built this revenue effect into the financial case below, but it represents meaningful upside.

4. Costs
Kiosks cost £14,500 each including the scanning scale and payment terminal. At six kiosks per store, the hardware cost is £87,000 per store, or £1,218,000 for 14 stores. Installation, electrical work and fit-out are quoted at £9,000 per store, a further £126,000, giving total capital of £1,344,000.

Ongoing maintenance and software licensing are quoted at £4,800 per store per year, or £67,200 across the 14 stores.

5. Savings
We assume each new store achieves the same 95-hour weekly reduction as the pilot stores, which is about 12% of a typical store's front-end hours. At a fully loaded front-end cost of £15.20 per hour, this is £1,444 per store per week, or £75,088 per store per year. Across 14 stores, gross labour savings are £1,051,232 per year.

After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432. Against capital of £1,344,000, the investment pays back in about 14 months, well inside the group's 24-month hurdle for store equipment.

6. Risks
Supply. The vendor has confirmed lead times of eight weeks, consistent with completion in Q3.

Customer acceptance. Older customers in some rural stores may prefer staffed lanes. Every store will keep at least two staffed lanes, and a colleague will be assigned to the kiosk bank at peak times, as in the pilot.

Labour transition. As in the pilot, reductions will be achieved through turnover and redeployment rather than redundancy. Annual front-end staff turnover across the estate is 38%, well above the 12% reduction in hours required, so we do not expect to need a consultation process.

7. Recommendation
The pilot has shown that self-checkout cuts peak queue times by more than half, holds shrink flat, improves customer satisfaction and lifts basket value, while delivering labour savings that repay the investment in little over a year. We recommend that the Committee approve capital of £1.34 million and a rollout to all 14 remaining stores, sequenced by store size, to complete by the end of September 2026.
</document>
response:
# Review: Self-Checkout Expansion Business Case

The case is clearly structured and the capital costing is correct. However, the net savings figure has an arithmetic error that overstates the return. The paper also extrapolates from a pilot that is unlikely to represent the remaining stores. Neither problem necessarily overturns the recommendation, but both should be fixed before this goes to the Committee.

## Errors to correct

**1. Net savings are wrong (Section 5).** Maintenance has been *added* to gross savings instead of subtracted:

- Stated: £1,051,232 → £1,118,432 (+£67,200)
- Correct: £1,051,232 − £67,200 = **£984,032 per year**

Payback becomes £1,344,000 ÷ £984,032 ≈ **16.4 months**, not "about 14 months." This is still inside the 24-month hurdle, so the conclusion holds. But the Committee will likely spot the error, and it undermines confidence in the rest of the numbers. The recommendation's phrase "little over a year" also needs updating.

**2. "Across the three pilot stores" (Section 3).** There are four pilot stores, as stated in Sections 1 and 2.

All other arithmetic checks out: kiosks £1,218,000, installation £126,000, total £1,344,000, maintenance £67,200, and labour at £1,444 per week, £75,088 per year and £1,051,232 across 14 stores.

## Substantive weaknesses

**3. The pilot stores are not representative.** They were chosen because they had just been refurbished and had spare floor space. The remaining 14 stores, by definition, lack one or both of these. This raises three problems:
- **Labour savings may not transfer.** If the remaining stores are smaller or more rural, they may have fewer front-end hours to remove. They may also be unable to fit six kiosks. The savings assume an identical 95-hour cut everywhere. The paper should show savings scaled to each store's front-end hours, or at least a sensitivity case.
- **Installation costs may be understated.** A flat £9,000 per store reflects stores that needed no shelving removed. Stores needing layout changes will cost more, and lost shelf space carries a sales cost.
- **Customer acceptance risk is greater** in the rural stores the paper itself flags.

**4. The basket value claim is not supported.** The pilot stores were refurbished just before the pilot. A refurbishment alone would plausibly lift basket value and front-end satisfaction. Saying the 6% vs 2% gap "shows" that faster checkout makes customers buy more is a causal claim the data can't support.

The paper rightly excludes this effect from the financials, but it then lists basket value as a proven benefit in the Recommendation. I'd soften this to "basket value rose faster in pilot stores, though refurbishment may account for some or all of this." The same caveat applies, to a lesser degree, to the satisfaction gain.

**5. Savings are assumed from day one.** The pilot reached −95 hours over ten months through natural turnover. The payback calculation assumes the full saving immediately after installation. A realistic ramp-up would lengthen payback beyond 16 months. It's worth modelling, since the margin to the 24-month hurdle is now smaller.

**6. The labour transition argument is too aggregate.** Estate-wide turnover of 38% doesn't guarantee enough leavers in each store at the right time. The pilot also relied on redeployment into online picking. Can online picking absorb staff from 14 more stores? If not, the "no consultation" assumption needs a fallback.

## Smaller points

- **No asset life, depreciation, NPV or contingency.** Kiosk life and replacement or refresh costs matter for a comparison with a 24-month payback. A contingency line (typically 5–10%) on capital would be expected.
- **Is the peak-time kiosk colleague netted off?** It's worth stating that the 95-hour figure is net of the colleague assigned to the kiosk bank.
- **Shrink evidence is short-term.** Ten months is a reasonable early read, but self-checkout losses often grow as customers learn where controls are weak. Ongoing monitoring should be part of the rollout.
- **The timeline is tight.** Approval, eight-week lead time and 14 installations by end of September leave little slack. A phased schedule would help.
- **The savings basis is conservative, which helps the case.** The −95 hours ignores the +3 hour drift in control stores, so the true relative saving is about 98 hours. You could note this as a modest offset to the risks above.

## Suggested priority

Fix items 1 and 2 before circulation. Address items 3 and 5 with a store-by-store or sensitivity view, because they are the most likely Committee challenges. Reword the basket value claims (item 4).
